scene-u01.name: Pattern Recognition Week 3 KP09 Least Squares (expert-first, English)

p01-matrix-title.name: p01-matrix-title
p01-matrix-title.text: The data are all in: put each sample in one row of a matrix and write the total error as one formula

p01-matrix-ctx.name: p01-matrix-ctx
p01-matrix-ctx.text: KP08 corrected one sample at a time. Now all $N$ data points are at hand and can be handled at once. Three samples of Example 3.4 illustrate (10 in all).

p01-matrix-src.name: p01-matrix-src
p01-matrix-src.text: Source: KP09 lecture §1 and Example 3.4 ($5$ points per class, augmented to $(x_1,x_2,1)$; the first $5$ targets are $+1$, the last $5$ are $-1$). Three rows are taken here to show the layout.

p01-matrix-c0.name: p01-matrix-c0
p01-matrix-c0.text: Each sample is a row of $X$ and the targets go in the vector $\mathbf y$.

p01-matrix-c1.name: p01-matrix-c1
p01-matrix-c1.text: Row 1: $\mathbf a_1^T=(0.2,\,0.7,\,1)$, target $y_1=+1$. Prediction $\widehat y_1=\mathbf a_1^T\mathbf w$.

p01-matrix-c2.name: p01-matrix-c2
p01-matrix-c2.text: Row 2 likewise; $\widehat{\mathbf y}=X\mathbf w$ computes all $N$ predictions at once. Residual vector $\mathbf e=\mathbf y-X\mathbf w$.

p01-matrix-c3.name: p01-matrix-c3
p01-matrix-c3.text: Row 6 is a negative sample with target $y=-1$. Together the 10 samples make $X$ a $10\times3$ matrix and $\mathbf y$ has 10 numbers.

p01-matrix-c4.name: p01-matrix-c4
p01-matrix-c4.text: The total error is the sum of all squared residuals: $J(\mathbf w)=\sum_i(y_i-\mathbf a_i^T\mathbf w)^2=\|\mathbf y-X\mathbf w\|^2$. Dividing by the fixed $N$ gives the empirical MSE; both have the same minimizing weights.

p02-small-title.name: p02-small-title
p02-small-title.text: Solve the normal equation: three points, one best-fitting line

p02-small-ctx.name: p02-small-ctx
p02-small-ctx.text: Data $(x,y)=(0,0),(1,1),(2,1)$, model $\widehat y=w_1x+w_2$. Set the gradient of $J$ to 0: $X^TX\mathbf w=X^T\mathbf y$.

p02-small-src.name: p02-small-src
p02-small-src.text: Source: KP09 lecture §2: $\nabla J=-2X^T(\mathbf y-X\mathbf w)$, zero gradient gives the normal equation and implies $X^T\mathbf e=\mathbf 0$; the three points are this page's teaching example (the lecture's practice uses a different data set).

p02-small-c0.name: p02-small-c0
p02-small-c0.text: The three points are not on one line, so no line passes through all of them. Which line makes the sum of squared residuals smallest?

p02-small-c3.name: p02-small-c3
p02-small-c3.text: The orange dashed lines are the residual $\mathbf e=(-0.167,\,0.333,\,-0.167)$. Residuals are positive and negative and their sum cancels to $0$.

p02-small-c4.name: p02-small-c4
p02-small-c4.text: Check $X^T\mathbf e=\mathbf 0$: $\sum e_i=0$, $\sum x_ie_i=0(-0.167)+1(0.333)+2(-0.167)=0$. The residual is perpendicular to every column of $X$ (back to KP07's projection).

p03-rank-title.name: p03-rank-title
p03-rank-title.text: When two columns are identical the answer is not unique: the pseudoinverse picks the "shortest" one

p03-rank-ctx.name: p03-rank-ctx
p03-rank-ctx.text: Data with two identical columns: sample 1 $(1,1)\to1$, sample 2 $(2,2)\to2$. $X^TX$ is not invertible. Draw the $(w_1,w_2)$ plane.

p03-rank-src.name: p03-rank-src
p03-rank-src.text: Source: KP09 lecture §3: $(X^TX)^{-1}X^T$ is the pseudoinverse only for full-rank columns; in general the Moore–Penrose one picks the minimum-norm solution (lecture [supplement] duplicated-column example).

p03-rank-c0.name: p03-rank-c0
p03-rank-c0.text: $\widehat y=w_1+w_2$ (the two columns are identical, so only $w_1+w_2$ matters). Which $\mathbf w$ make $\widehat{\mathbf y}=\mathbf y$ hold exactly?

p03-rank-c1.name: p03-rank-c1
p03-rank-c1.text: Every point on the green line $w_1+w_2=1$ fits exactly with error 0. There are infinitely many solutions: $X^TX$ is not invertible, $(X^TX)^{-1}$ does not exist.

p03-rank-c2.name: p03-rank-c2
p03-rank-c2.text: $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ are both on the line, with squared length $1$ (gray circle). Is there a point on the line nearer the origin?

p03-rank-c3.name: p03-rank-c3
p03-rank-c3.text: The point nearest the origin is $(0.5,0.5)$ with squared length $0.5$ (red circle). The pseudoinverse $X^+\mathbf y$ picks exactly it: the smallest norm among all least-squares solutions.

p03-rank-c4.name: p03-rank-c4
p03-rank-c4.text: So $(X^TX)^{-1}X^T$ is the pseudoinverse only when "columns are full rank"; in general use the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. The prediction $\widehat{\mathbf y}$ is still unique, only the weights are not.

p04-example-title.name: p04-example-title
p04-example-title.text: Example 3.4: the least-squares solution for ten points and the line it draws

p04-example-ctx.name: p04-example-ctx
p04-example-ctx.text: Blue circles are ω₁ (target $+1$), red triangles ω₂ (target $-1$). After augmenting, $X$ is $10\times3$.

p04-example-src.name: p04-example-src
p04-example-src.text: Source: KP09 lecture Example 3.4: $X^TX$, $X^T\mathbf y$, $\widehat{\mathbf w}=(-3.218,0.241,1.431)$ (computed with unrounded weights); recomputed by build_kp09_en.py and independently by check_numbers_kp09.py.

p04-example-c0.name: p04-example-c0
p04-example-c0.text: The 10 points' blue circles and red triangles overlap. Fit a line by least squares: what is the result?

p04-example-c2.name: p04-example-c2
p04-example-c2.text: Solving the normal equation: $\widehat{\mathbf w}=(-3.218,\,0.241,\,1.431)$ (as fractions $\tfrac{-4000}{1243},\tfrac{300}{1243},\tfrac{1779}{1243}$).

p04-example-c3.name: p04-example-c3
p04-example-c3.text: The green line $g=0$; the background blue: predict positive, red: predict negative.

p04-example-c4.name: p04-example-c4
p04-example-c4.text: Red circles: $(0.6,0.5)$ has target $+1$ yet $g=-0.378922<0$; $(0.4,0.6)$ has target $-1$ yet $g=0.288817>0$. These two are misclassified. The sum of the 10 squared residuals $=4.827031376$.

p05-midpoint-title.name: p05-midpoint-title
p05-midpoint-title.text: "This line misclassifies" does not prove non-separability; the real evidence is the "midpoint"

p05-midpoint-ctx.name: p05-midpoint-ctx
p05-midpoint-ctx.text: The negative point $(0.4,0.6)$ is exactly the midpoint of the two positive points $(0.2,0.7)$ and $(0.6,0.5)$.

p05-midpoint-src.name: p05-midpoint-src
p05-midpoint-src.text: Source: KP09 lecture [supplementary check]: the score $g$ of any line is an affine function; if both ends are positive, the midpoint is positive; so a negative midpoint can never be classified correctly by any line.

p05-midpoint-c0.name: p05-midpoint-c0
p05-midpoint-c0.text: The LS line errs, which only says "this one" is bad. Could another line classify them all correctly? First look for a geometric clue.

p05-midpoint-c1.name: p05-midpoint-c1
p05-midpoint-c1.text: Join the two positive points $(0.2,0.7)$ and $(0.6,0.5)$. Their midpoint is $(0.4,0.6)$ (gold point), exactly the negative point.

p05-midpoint-c2.name: p05-midpoint-c2
p05-midpoint-c2.text: The score of any line $g(\mathbf x)=\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+b$ is an affine function: $g(\text{midpoint})=\tfrac12\,[g(\mathbf p)+g(\mathbf q)]$. With $g>0$ at both ends, the midpoint's $g$ must also be $>0$.

p05-midpoint-c3.name: p05-midpoint-c3
p05-midpoint-c3.text: But the midpoint is negative and needs $g<0$. Contradiction: no line classifies all 10 points correctly. The data are not linearly separable, proved geometrically, not because the LS line errs.

p05-midpoint-c4.name: p05-midpoint-c4
p05-midpoint-c4.text: The converse is also true: "linear separability" cannot be judged by whether LS classifies correctly.

p06-score-vs-error-title.name: p06-score-vs-error-title
p06-score-vs-error-title.text: Least squares minimizes "how far the scores are from ±1", not "how many are misclassified"

p06-score-vs-error-ctx.name: p06-score-vs-error-ctx
p06-score-vs-error-ctx.text: Put the 10 points' scores $g_i=\mathbf a_i^T\widehat{\mathbf w}$ on a number line. Blue: target $+1$, red: target $-1$.

p06-score-vs-error-src.name: p06-score-vs-error-src
p06-score-vs-error-src.text: Source: KP09 lecture §5 "common myths"; the 10 scores are computed by build_kp09_en.py with unrounded weights, sum of squared residuals $4.827031376$.

p06-score-vs-error-c0.name: p06-score-vs-error-c0
p06-score-vs-error-c0.text: Where do the 10 scores fall? Which are on the wrong side of the boundary $g=0$?

p06-score-vs-error-c1.name: p06-score-vs-error-c1
p06-score-vs-error-c1.text: Blue points (target $+1$): mostly right of 0, but $(0.6,0.5)$ with $g=-0.379$ lands on the left (misclassified).

p06-score-vs-error-c2.name: p06-score-vs-error-c2
p06-score-vs-error-c2.text: Red triangles (target $−1$): mostly left of 0, but $(0.4,0.6)$ with $g=0.289$ lands on the right (misclassified).

p06-score-vs-error-c3.name: p06-score-vs-error-c3
p06-score-vs-error-c3.text: Squared error looks at $|y-g|$, not the sign: the squared distances of blue points from $+1$ and red points from $-1$ add up to $4.827$. Moving a misclassified point to the right side does not necessarily make this sum smaller.

p06-score-vs-error-c4.name: p06-score-vs-error-c4
p06-score-vs-error-c4.text: In practice: solve directly with `np.linalg.lstsq` (it handles underdetermined and rank-deficient cases), then recompute the residual yourself with `y - X@w`; do not form the matrix inverse explicitly first.

p07-practice-title.name: p07-practice-title
p07-practice-title.text: Practice: x = (1, 2, 3), y = (1, $−1$, $−1$): build the matrix, solve for the weights, check Xᵀe

p07-practice-ctx.name: p07-practice-ctx
p07-practice-ctx.text: Work it out first. Hint: the last column is all 1s; write the two equations $X^TX$ and $X^T\mathbf y$ first and then solve. Press Next when done.

p07-practice-src.name: p07-practice-src
p07-practice-src.text: Source: KP09 lecture practice; answer computed by build_kp09_en.py ($\mathbf w=(-1,5/3)$) and recomputed independently by check_numbers_kp09.py.

p07-practice-q.name: p07-practice-q
p07-practice-q.text: (a) The design matrix $X$ ($3\times2$)? (b) Solve $X^TX\mathbf w=X^T\mathbf y$ for $\mathbf w$? (c) The residual $\mathbf e$, and check $X^T\mathbf e$.

p07-practice-a4.name: p07-practice-a4
p07-practice-a4.text: The residual is perpendicular to both columns of $X$ ($x$ and all ones), the signature of the LS solution.

p08-summary-title.name: p08-summary-title
p08-summary-title.text: Summary: solve finite data directly; normal equation; pseudoinverse; LS is not the classification optimum

p08-summary-ctx.name: p08-summary-ctx
p08-summary-ctx.text: Recall along Example 3.4; the five conclusions of this KP are on the right.

p08-summary-e0.name: p08-summary-e0
p08-summary-e0.text: Each row of $X$ is one sample: $J=\|\mathbf y-X\mathbf w\|^2$ (same solution as the empirical MSE)

p08-summary-e1.name: p08-summary-e1
p08-summary-e1.text: Zero gradient: $X^TX\mathbf w=X^T\mathbf y$, and $X^T\mathbf e=\mathbf 0$ (the residual is perpendicular to every column)

p08-summary-e2.name: p08-summary-e2
p08-summary-e2.text: Full-rank columns: $\mathbf w=(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf y$ is unique; duplicated columns: the pseudoinverse picks the minimum-norm solution

p08-summary-e3.name: p08-summary-e3
p08-summary-e3.text: The LS line may misclassify; misclassification does not prove non-separability (use the midpoint argument); squared error ≠ classification error

p08-summary-e4.name: p08-summary-e4
p08-summary-e4.text: Open question: if we do not restrict to a line, what is the best prediction? Next KP: the conditional expectation

p02-normal-derive-title.text: Where the normal equations come from: expand the square, differentiate in $\mathbf w$, set the gradient to zero
p02-normal-derive-title.name: p02-normal-derive-title

p02-normal-derive-ctx.text: Continuing from the last page: $J(\mathbf w)=\|\mathbf y-X\mathbf w\|^2$. Expand the square first, then differentiate in $\mathbf w$.
p02-normal-derive-ctx.name: p02-normal-derive-ctx

p02-normal-derive-src.text: Source: KP09 lecture §2 (zero gradient gives the normal equations); the example reuses the three-point data of the next page ($\mathbf y=(0,1,1)$), recomputed independently. Added page: the original deck used the normal equations directly, restored derivation from the lecture.
p02-normal-derive-src.name: p02-normal-derive-src

p02-normal-derive-th.text: $J(\mathbf w)$ for three candidate weights on the same data
p02-normal-derive-th.name: p02-normal-derive-th

p02-normal-derive-c0.text: $J(\mathbf w)=(\mathbf y-X\mathbf w)^T(\mathbf y-X\mathbf w)=\mathbf y^T\mathbf y-2\mathbf w^TX^T\mathbf y+\mathbf w^TX^TX\mathbf w$. (The two cross terms are equal and merge into $-2\mathbf w^TX^T\mathbf y$.)
p02-normal-derive-c0.name: p02-normal-derive-c0

p02-normal-derive-c1.text: Differentiate in $\mathbf w$: the constant vanishes, the linear term gives $-2X^T\mathbf y$, the quadratic term gives $2X^TX\mathbf w$, so $\nabla J(\mathbf w)=-2X^T(\mathbf y-X\mathbf w)$. The minus sign comes from differentiating $\mathbf y-X\mathbf w$ in $\mathbf w$.
p02-normal-derive-c1.name: p02-normal-derive-c1

p02-normal-derive-c2.text: Set the gradient to zero: $\nabla J(\hat{\mathbf w})=\mathbf 0\Longrightarrow X^TX\hat{\mathbf w}=X^T\mathbf y$ (the normal equations), that is $X^T\mathbf e=\mathbf 0$: the residual is perpendicular to every column of $X$, linking back to the projection of KP07.
p02-normal-derive-c2.name: p02-normal-derive-c2

p02-normal-derive-c3.text: Check (three-point data $\mathbf y=(0,1,1)$): at $\mathbf w=(0,0)$, $J=2$ with gradient $(-6,-4)$; at $\mathbf w=(1,0)$, $J=1$ with gradient $(4,2)$; at $\hat{\mathbf w}=(0.5,0.1667)$, $J=0.1667$ with gradient $(0,0)$, the lowest.
p02-normal-derive-c3.name: p02-normal-derive-c3

p02-normal-derive-c4.text: If the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, $X^TX$ is invertible and $\hat{\mathbf w}=(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf y$ is unique (used on the next page); with repeated columns $X^TX$ is singular and the pseudoinverse is needed (page 3).
p02-normal-derive-c4.name: p02-normal-derive-c4

p02-normal-derive-cue1.text: See the blue card: differentiate in $\mathbf w$.
p02-normal-derive-cue1.name: p02-normal-derive-cue1

p02-normal-derive-cue2.text: See the green card: set the gradient to zero.
p02-normal-derive-cue2.name: p02-normal-derive-cue2

p02-normal-derive-cue3.text: See the three bars: only at $\hat{\mathbf w}$ is the gradient zero and $J$ lowest.
p02-normal-derive-cue3.name: p02-normal-derive-cue3

p02-normal-derive-cue4.text: See the gold star: invertible and singular.
p02-normal-derive-cue4.name: p02-normal-derive-cue4
